blocks.text: The oldest Venus figurine found in Austria is not the famous Venus of Willendorf. It is the Venus of Galgenberg, estimated to be 66,000 years old, and it now rests in the Natural History Museum in Vienna. Most people know the Willendorf figure, but the Galgenberg one is far older, and it holds the title for being the earliest of its kind discovered on Austrian soil. For years, the discovery of Ötzi the Iceman seemed like a modern legend.

In 1991, hikers in the Ötztal Alps stumbled upon a glacier mummy that turned out to be around 5,300 years old, making it the oldest known natural human mummy in Europe. Today, Ötzi is preserved and displayed at the South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology in Bolzano. When the Romans expanded their empire, they divided their territory into provinces. Of the four provinces named in the question, three were located on today’s Austrian land: Raetia covered parts of Vorarlberg and Tyrol, Noricum included much of central Austria, and Pannonia held Vienna, parts of Lower Austria, and Burgenland.

The one that was not on Austrian soil was Gaul, which lay far to the west. Salzburg had a unique form of rule for centuries. In 798, the Archdiocese of Salzburg was founded, and from that point onward, the sovereign of the territory was also its archbishop. This dual role remained in place until Salzburg was eventually brought under Habsburg control. Before Austria became an independent duchy, it was subordinate to Bavaria. The territory belonged to the Duchy of Bavaria and was governed from there until the political landscape of the region shifted. Vienna, which we know today as a bustling capital, was quiet for a long time after the Romans abandoned the camp of Vindobona in the 5th century. It was not until the year 881 that Vienna was first mentioned in a document, specifically in the Salzburg Annals, where a battle against the Magyars took place “aput vena,” meaning at Vienna. Historians are still unsure whether that reference points to the city itself or to the Vienna River. The first independent duchy in what would become Austria was Carinthia. Because of a dispute with the rebellious Duke of Bavaria, the Emperor of the Holy Roman Empire reduced the duke’s territory and established Carinthia as its own duchy in 976. Austria itself was first mentioned in a document in the year 996, through the so-called Ostarrichi Document.

That document famously references a region commonly called Ostarrichi, which would eventually evolve into the name Austria. Before the Habsburgs took power, the dynasty that ruled Austria for about two hundred years was the Babenbergers. Emperor Otto installed them as Margraves in the East in 976. The last male Babenberger died in 1246, after which the territory passed to the Bohemian King Ottokar II. One of the Babenbergers was later canonized. Leopold III, who lived in the 12th century and was buried in his abbey at Klosterneuburg, was canonized in the 15th century. He went on to become the patron saint of Vienna and Lower Austria. Austria was elevated to a duchy in 1156 through a document called the Privilegium Minus. This came after yet another dispute between the Duke of Bavaria and the King of the Holy Roman Empire, and it separated Austria from Bavarian territory, establishing it as an independent duchy under the Babenbergers. The document also granted Austria many additional privileges. About a hundred years later, a Privilegium Majus would be created, building upon the foundations of the earlier document. Styria joined Austria in 1192.

The Georgenberg Pact, signed in 1186 between the Babenberger Leopold V and the Styrian Duke Ottokar IV, stipulated that after the duke’s death, Styria would pass to the Babenbergers. The inheritance took place in 1192. When it comes to the oldest non-ancient town charter in Austria, the answer is Enns. As early as 1212, Enns received its own town charter, making it the oldest of its kind in the country. The Battle of Dürnkrut and Jedenspeigen in 1278 marks the beginning of Habsburg rule in Austria. In that battle, Rudolf I, the first king of the Habsburg dynasty, defeated Ottokar II, who died on the field. After that victory, the Austrian territories went to the Habsburg family. Construction of St. Stephen’s Cathedral began in 1137, made possible by the Mautern exchange agreement, which swapped territories in Vienna between the duke and the Bishop of Passau. The last Countess of Tyrol was Margarete, sometimes known by the mocking name “Maultasch. ” She outlived both her husband and her son, and in the 14th century, she handed Tyrol over to the Habsburgs. Because she did so rather than letting it pass to her late husband’s Bavarian family, Bavarian chroniclers disparaged her for centuries with that unflattering nickname, which she has never been able to shake off.

The University of Vienna, founded in 1365 by Duke Rudolf IV, is recognized as the oldest German-speaking university still in existence today. It was not the first one ever established, but it is the oldest one that has survived continuously. Austria was elevated to an archduchy under Emperor Frederick III. He was the first Habsburg to receive the imperial title, and in the 15th century, he confirmed the Privilegium Majus, which raised the Habsburgs to the rank of archdukes. The first Ottoman siege of Vienna took place in 1529. The Ottomans stood before the city but withdrew without achieving their goal. In 1683, they tried again, but this time they were driven off by a relief force made up of troops from the Holy Roman Empire and Polish units. After that second failure, the Habsburgs began conquering large territories in the east that had previously been ruled by the Ottoman Empire. The military commander who ultimately pushed the Ottomans back to Serbia, giving the Habsburg Empire its greatest expansion, was Prince Eugene of Savoy. He came from a French noble family, but because he was not accepted into the French army, he entered the service of the Habsburgs and rose to become one of the most successful commanders in their history. Compulsory education was introduced in Austria in 1774. Under the regent Maria Theresa, compulsory instruction, rather than compulsory school attendance, was established across the Austrian lands.

The oldest zoo still in existence in the world is Schönbrunn Zoo. It was founded in 1752 by Maria Theresa’s husband, Francis Stephen. Several famous musicians are buried in Vienna, but not all of them were born in what is now Austria. Ludwig van Beethoven, for example, was born in Bonn in 1770. He moved to Vienna at the age of 22 and died there in 1827. Today, he is buried in the musicians’ section of the Vienna Central Cemetery. Torture and the death penalty were first abolished in Austria in the 18th century, during the lifetime of Maria Theresa. In the late 1770s, both were done away with in the Austrian lands, though they were later reintroduced. The last death sentence carried out by an Austrian court was in 1950. The sentence was imposed on Johann Trinker, a robber and murderer. The Allies, however, maintained military jurisdiction in Austria at the time. It was not until 1968 that the National Council finally decided to abolish the death penalty in Austria for good.

The Austrian Empire was born in 1804. Emperor Franz I, who was also Franz II of the Holy Roman Empire, elevated Austria to an empire in 1804. Two years later, in 1806, he dissolved the Holy Roman Empire. For those two years, he held both titles: Emperor Franz II of the Holy Roman Empire and Emperor Franz I of Austria. Salzburg was integrated into the Habsburg-Austrian lands in 1814. At the Congress of Vienna, which ran from 1814 to 1815, Europe was reorganized after the turmoil of the Napoleonic era. In the course of those negotiations, Salzburg joined Austria and ceased to be an independent archbishopric. Austria’s oldest and most important naval port was Trieste. As early as 1382, Trieste voluntarily submitted to the Habsburgs, and from then on, it served as a crucial gateway to the Adriatic. The division into the dual monarchy of Austria-Hungary took place in 1867. In that year, Emperor Franz Joseph had to grant significant privileges to the Hungarians in what became known as the Austro-Hungarian Compromise. The Hungarians received their own parliament, and the dual monarchy of Austria-Hungary was created.

The first female doctor allowed to study medicine in Austria was Margarete Hönigsberg. In 1903, she became the first woman to earn a doctorate after completing a full medical degree in Vienna. Before her, Gabriele Possanner had opened her practice in 1897 as the first independent female general practitioner in Vienna, but she had earned her doctorate in Switzerland because women were not permitted to study medicine in Austria at that time. Three years later, in 1900, women were finally admitted to medical studies in Austria. The Austrian €2 coin features Bertha von Suttner. She advocated for peace with her work “Lay Down Your Arms,” and in 1905, she became the first woman to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. Despite her efforts, she could not prevent the Great War. She died a few weeks before the outbreak of World War I. The event that triggered the First World War was the assassination of the heir to the throne, Franz Ferdinand. On June 28, 1914, he was murdered in Sarajevo. After that, Emperor Franz Joseph signed the declaration of war against Serbia, and one country after another entered the conflict, which grew to a scale no one had foreseen. The peace treaty for Austria was signed in 1919 in Saint-Germain.

The peace treaties for Hungary were signed in Trianon, those for Turkey in Sèvres, and the one for Germany in Versailles. The republic was proclaimed on November 12, 1918. On that day, the Republic of German-Austria was declared. However, the peace treaty of Saint-Germain later mandated that the country be called the Republic of Austria. Since 1919, noble titles have been completely banned in Austria. In April of that year, the Law on the Abolition of Nobility was passed, which prohibited noble titles and privileges. That law still holds constitutional rank in Austria today. The first State Chancellor of the newborn republic was Karl Renner. A Social Democrat, he played a key role in building the new republic as State Chancellor from 1918 to 1920. After the Second World War and the occupation period, he even became the first Federal President of the Second Republic. The youngest of the Austrian federal states, in constitutional terms, is Burgenland. On December 5, 1921, it was officially handed over from Hungary to Austria.

Vienna is often mistakenly named as the youngest, but Vienna was already defined as a separate state by the Federal Constitutional Law that came into force on November 10, 1920. The separation law regarding its final financial split from Lower Austria only came into force in 1922, which is why Vienna is often cited as the youngest. The Burgenland is actually called that because of the Hungarian counties. The name was a new creation after the First World War, and it serves as a reminder that the region was composed of parts of four old Hungarian counties, all of which had “burg,” meaning castle, in their names: Eisenburg, Ödenburg, Wieselburg, and Pressburg. Ironically, all four of those namesake castles now lie on Hungarian or Slovakian territory. The annexation of Austria to the German Reich took place on March 12, 1938. The National Socialists invaded, and Austria was incorporated into the German Reich. From 1939 to 1942, Austria was called Ostmark. On March 15, 1938, Adolf Hitler announced the entry of Austria into the German Reich at Heldenplatz in Vienna. He referred to Austria as the oldest Ostmark of the German people. The term Ostmark was used until 1942, after which the region was referred to as the Alpine and Danube districts. During World War II, Wiener Neustadt suffered the most bomb damage of any Austrian city in percentage terms.

Because of its concentration of armaments factories and its importance as a railway junction, the city was almost completely destroyed by around 50,000 bombs. Out of 3,000 buildings, only 18 remained intact. The Second Republic was born, and Austria became a sovereign state again, on May 15, 1955. After ten years of occupation, Austria regained its sovereignty through the signing of the State Treaty. The State Treaty was signed at the Belvedere Palace, specifically in the Marble Hall of the Upper Belvedere. Austrian National Day is October 26. On that day in 1955, the first day came when no occupying soldier remained on Austrian soil. Also on that day, the Austrian Neutrality Act was passed, making Austria a militarily neutral state to this day. The federal state that has no animal in its coat of arms is Vorarlberg. Its coat of arms dates back to the medieval House of Montfort. Vienna officially has two versions, one without an eagle and one with one. The youngest state capital in Austria is St.

Pölten. It became the capital of Lower Austria by a provincial parliament resolution on July 10, 1986. Until that point, Vienna had served as the capital of Lower Austria. Austria joined the European Union, or the European Community as it was then called, in 1995. On June 12, 1994, a referendum was held on the country’s accession, and it was approved with 66. 6 percent of the vote. Austria’s accession therefore took place the following year. The currency Austria had right before the euro was the schilling. From 1925 to 1938 and from 1945 to 1998, the schilling was used as both book money and cash. From 1999 until the introduction of the euro as cash in 2002, the schilling existed only as cash. The place in Upper Austria that is a major destination, especially for Asian tourists, is Hallstatt. The market town has fewer than 800 inhabitants, yet it attracts over a million tourists every year because of its idyllic location between the lake and the mountains.

The lyrics to the Austrian national anthem were written by Paula von Preradović. Her text emerged as the winner of a government competition, and by cabinet decision on February 25, 1947, the national anthem was officially introduced.
